--- title: "Bayesian estimation" subtitle: "Extended course – day 3" format: revealjs # Optional runs that this deck includes in its main flow (core-runs.lua # strips their .deepdive mark); the others stay on the d toggle. This deck # has no optional runs. core-runs: [] --- ## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.todaymeta} Session 3 of day 3, on the slope of the claim as a posterior distribution ::: :::: {.todaybox} ::: {.nonincremental .fs-85} 1. Priors and the posterior – what the priors imply before the data enter, the posterior of the two-way slope, and the checks of its computation 2. Persistence within countries – the posterior predictive check, and errors that persist from one year to the next 3. Partial pooling – a slope for each country, each estimated partly from the others 4. The result – the sensitivity to the priors, the slope across the models, and the probability of a negative slope ::: :::: ::: {.todaytake .fs-85} You leave able to read a posterior distribution, to say what its priors imply, and to judge what a Bayesian model adds when 27 countries carry the evidence ::: ::: {.todaymeta} The models were fitted once, with brms; you work in the workspace, in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) ::: ::: notes The third session goes back to the panel and estimates the slope of the claim by Bayesian methods. Nothing about the data changes, but the slope becomes a distribution, about which we can make direct statements of probability, and the dependence of the years of a country, which the CR2 test repairs after the fit, has to be written into the model itself. We take the steps in the order of the Bayesian workflow. First the priors and what they imply before the data enter, then the posterior of the two-way slope and the checks that its computation worked. Then the model fails a check against the data, and we take two readings of the failure: errors that persist within a country, and partial pooling, which gives every country a slope of its own. Last, the sensitivity to the priors, and the slope across all the models. The models take a while to fit, so they were fitted once, and the slides read their results. ::: # PART 1 – Priors and the posterior {#part-1-priors .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 1 ::: ::: notes Part one builds the model and reads its first result. We start with the three pieces of any Bayesian analysis, the prior, the likelihood and the posterior, on a model that you know from the last session. Then the priors of the two-way design, stated on scales that everyone can read, a simulation of what the priors imply before the data enter, and your first run of the session, a prior simulated by hand. The part ends with the posterior of the two-way slope and the checks that the computation behind it worked. ::: ## Prior, likelihood and posterior {#prior-likelihood-and-posterior .smaller} $$ p(\theta \mid y) \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\; p(\theta) $$ ::: {.small} - The **prior** says which values of the parameters are plausible before the data enter, the **likelihood** how probable the data are under each value, and the **posterior** is a distribution over all the parameters at once - Markov chain Monte Carlo draws thousands of values whose frequencies match the posterior, and inference summarises the draws: a median, an interval that holds 95% of them, the share of them below zero - brms fits Bayesian regressions through Stan, with the formula syntax of `lmer()` [@Burkner2017BrmsPackageBayesian] ::: ```{.r} brms::brm(mcosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | year), data = euframes, backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, iter = 4000, seed = 2026) ``` ::: {.fragment .small} With the default priors of brms, the standard deviation of the year intercepts has a posterior mean of 0.0184 and a 95% credible interval from 0.0094 to 0.0333, a statement of how little ten years can establish about a variance between years. ::: ::: {.src} companion/bayesian.qmd, section 1; companion/_model-outputs/bayes_panel.R and bayes_panel_summary.csv. ::: ::: notes A Bayesian analysis starts from a prior, a distribution that says which values of the parameters are plausible before the data enter. The likelihood, the model read as a statement of how probable the data are under each value, updates the prior into a posterior, a distribution over all the parameters at once. For models like ours the posterior has no closed form, so Stan explores it by Markov chain Monte Carlo, drawing thousands of values whose frequencies match it. Inference is then a summary of the draws: a median, an interval that holds ninety-five per cent of them, the share of them below zero. brms speaks the formula language of lmer, so the first model is a familiar one, with random intercepts for countries and years. [advance] Its output adds what a Bayesian fit can say about a variance: ten years leave the spread of the years uncertain, anywhere between about one and three points of share. ::: ## Priors on readable scales {#priors-on-readable-scales .smaller} $$ \bar{y}_{ct} \sim N\!\left( \alpha_c + \gamma_t + \beta\,(x_{ct} - \bar{x}_{c\cdot}),\; \sigma^2 \right) $$ ::: {.small} - The two-way design of the reproduced specification, with unemployment as the departure of each year from the mean of its country over the decade - The level of each country takes normal(0.5, 0.15), a share between about 0.2 and 0.8 with 95% probability; the departure of each later year normal(0, 0.1); the residual standard deviation exponential(20), whose mean of 0.05 is a few points of share - The slope takes normal(0, 0.01): a rise of ten points of unemployment, about half of the rises of 17.9 points in Spain and 19.7 points in Greece, may move the share by up to about 0.2 either way - "Using scientific knowledge to build priors is not cheating. The important thing is that your prior not be based on the values in the data, but only on what you know about the data before you see it" [@McElreath2020StatisticalRethinkingBayesian, p. 84] ::: ::: notes From here on the models take the two-way design of the reproduced specification, so that the Bayesian slope answers the same question as the curve. A Bayesian model needs a prior for every parameter, and here the priors can be stated on scales that everyone can read: a share between nought and one, and a rate of unemployment in points. Each country gets a level of its own, centred on a half and allowed to range from about a fifth to four fifths. Each later year may depart from the first by a few points. The slope is centred on no effect, with room for a rise of ten points of unemployment, about half of what Spain and Greece went through, to move the share by up to about twenty points either way. McElreath states the principle behind such choices: using what you know before the data is not cheating, as long as the prior is not built from the values in the data. ::: ## What the priors imply {#what-the-priors-imply .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](eu-frames-bayesian_files/figure-revealjs/d3-prior-predictive-1.png){width=912} ::: ::: ::: {.small} - brms fits the model with the likelihood switched off when `sample_prior = "only"` is set, and `posterior_predict()` then draws cell means from the priors alone: "[t]he prior predictive simulation is an essential part of your modeling" [@McElreath2020StatisticalRethinkingBayesian, p. 82] - Before the data, 95% of the cell means lie between 0.11 and 0.88, and 1.1% fall outside the bounds of a share; a rise of ten points of unemployment changes the share by between −20 and +19 points ::: ::: notes What priors imply together is seldom obvious from the priors one by one, so the workflow simulates the outcome from the priors alone, before the data enter. brms does this when you ask it to sample from the prior only, and McElreath calls the prior predictive simulation an essential part of modelling. On the left are the cell means that the priors allow: a broad hump around a half, with about one per cent of the simulated means outside the bounds of a share, which a model with normal errors cannot avoid entirely and which is small enough to leave the model sensible. On the right is the change in the share that a rise of ten points of unemployment could bring, anything within about twenty points either way. That rules out nothing that a crisis could plausibly do to framing, and it keeps the slope away from values that no survey could produce. ::: ## Hands-on 1 – Simulating a prior {#hands-on-1-simulating-a-prior .smaller} ::: {.small} **In the workspace**, in the console: 1. Draw from the prior of the slope, and turn each draw into the change in the share, in points, for a rise of ten points of unemployment: ```{.r} set.seed(20261106) prior_draws <- tibble::tibble(slope = rnorm(4000, 0, 0.01)) |> datawizard::data_modify(rise_10 = 10 * 100 * slope) quantile(prior_draws$rise_10, c(0.025, 0.975)) tinyplot::tinyplot(~ rise_10, data = prior_draws, type = "histogram") ``` 2. Compare the interval with the right panel of the prior predictive check, then set the standard deviation of the slope to 0.001, and to 0.05 3. **Which standard deviation describes what you believed about the slope before you read the paper?** One sentence for your notes ::: ::: notes This is a prior predictive check done by hand, with base R and two packages from the workspace. Draw four thousand values of the slope from the normal prior with a standard deviation of point nought one, and turn each into the change in the cosmopolitan share, in points, that a rise of ten points of unemployment would bring. The interval should come close to the right panel of the last slide, about twenty points either way. Then narrow the prior to point nought nought one, which allows only about two points either way, and widen it to point nought five, which allows changes of almost the whole range of a share. The last question has no right answer, but answering it is what choosing a prior means. [state the time] ::: ## The posterior of the two-way slope {#the-posterior-of-the-two-way-slope .smaller} ::: {.small} - With one slope and independent errors, the model is the Bayesian form of the reproduced specification: posterior median **−0.00345**, 95% credible interval −0.00517 to −0.00169 - The least-squares slope is −0.00347 with a conventional standard error of 0.00091, so priors this weak are outweighed by 270 country-years - The probability that the slope is negative is 1 to the precision of the draws, since every draw lies below zero - A credible interval says that, given the model, the prior and the data, the slope lies within it with a probability of 95%, the statement that a confidence interval is often misread as making ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The likelihood treats the 270 country-years as independent, as the conventional standard error does, so the posterior inherits the assumption that the clustered errors of the first session correct. ::: ::: {.src} companion/bayesian.qmd, section 3; cases/eu-frames/data/display_inference.csv. ::: ::: notes With the data switched on and the errors of the country-years treated as independent, the model is the Bayesian form of the reproduced specification. The posterior median of the slope agrees closely with least squares, because priors this weak are outweighed by two hundred and seventy country-years. The credible interval makes the statement that a confidence interval is so often misread as making: given the model, the prior and the data, the slope lies inside it with a probability of ninety-five per cent. And every one of the draws lies below zero. [advance] That agreement is also the limitation of the model. Its likelihood treats the 270 rows as independent pieces of evidence, exactly as the conventional standard error did this morning, so the posterior inherits the assumption that the clustered errors were there to correct. ::: ## Computational checks {#computational-checks .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Model Draws R-hat Bulk ESS Tail ESS Divergences Tree depth
Random intercepts, default priors 8,000 1.003 818 1,322 0 7
Two-way, priors only 4,000 1.004 3,843 2,073 0 4
Two-way, one slope 4,000 1.005 509 1,006 0 5
Two-way, persistent errors 4,000 1.006 898 1,266 0 6
Two-way, a slope for each country 4,000 1.004 931 1,566 0 6
Two-way, country slopes and persistence 4,000 1.006 946 1,835 0 6
``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} The chains agree when R-hat is below 1.01, they carry enough independent information when the effective sample sizes exceed about 400, and the sampler explored the whole posterior when no transition diverged. ::: ::: notes Every number of this session assumes that the computation worked. Stan draws from the posterior with four chains that start in different places. R-hat asks whether the four chains agree; below one point nought one is the usual standard, and every model is inside it. The effective sample sizes ask how much independent information the correlated draws carry; above about four hundred is enough for the summaries that we use, and the smallest here is about five hundred. Divergent transitions flag regions of the posterior that the sampler could not explore, and there are none. The table already holds the three models of the next two parts. In the two with a slope for each country, the spread of those slopes can lie near zero, where the sampler needs small steps, which is why the script asked for a smaller step size in every two-way fit. The slope on the last slide counts only once these checks have passed, because a posterior from a computation that failed is not worth reading. ::: # PART 2 – Persistence within countries {#part-2-persistence .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 2 ::: ::: notes Part two takes the problem of the first session, few clusters of unequal weight, and asks what a Bayesian model does about it. The CR2 test repairs the standard errors after the fit. A Bayesian model has no such repair: the dependence of the years of a country has to be written into the model, and a posterior predictive check tells us whether it has been. The model of the first part fails that check. The part ends with a model whose errors persist from year to year, and with your second run, which fits the frequentist twin of that model. ::: ## The dependence of the years {#the-dependence-of-the-years .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="52%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](eu-frames-bayesian_files/figure-revealjs/d3-persistence-check-1.png){width=537.6} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.small} - "If the model fits, then replicated data generated under the model should look similar to observed data" [@GelmanEtAl2014BayesianDataAnalysis, p. 143] - The statistic: the persistence of the residuals, 0.53 in the data (red line) - With one slope, the replicated persistence has a median of −0.12, and no replicated dataset reaches the observed value - The two models with persistent errors pass ::: ::: :::: ::: notes A model that passes its computational checks may still fail to describe the data. The test is to let the fitted model generate new datasets and compare them with the real one on a statistic that matters, and Bayesian Data Analysis states the principle: replicated data should look like the observed data. The statistic here is the persistence of the residuals, the correlation of the first session, about a half in the data. Look at the top left. The model with one slope replicates a persistence near zero, slightly negative, and not one of its datasets reaches the observed value, because a model with independent errors cannot produce a country that stays above the expected value year after year. Only the two models in the bottom row, in which the errors persist from year to year, reproduce the persistence in the data. The two panels with a slope for each country belong to the third part, and we come back to them there. ::: ## Persistent errors {#persistent-errors .smaller} $$ e_{ct} = \phi\, e_{c,t-1} + \varepsilon_{ct}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ct} \sim N(0, \sigma^2) $$ ::: {.small} - The error of each year carries a fraction φ of the error of the year before, `ar(time = year, gr = cntry, p = 1, cov = TRUE)` in brms, under the prior normal(0, 0.5), which is centred on no persistence - φ has a posterior median of 0.77 (95% credible interval 0.63 to 0.88), and 37% of the replicated values of persistence lie above the observed one - The slope moves and widens, to a median of −0.00270 (95% credible interval −0.00506 to −0.00029): the likelihood compares each year with what the year before predicts, so the information comes more from the change from one year to the next ::: ::: notes The failed check names the next model. Let the error of each year carry a fraction phi of the error of the year before, a first-order autoregressive process within each country, with a prior on phi centred on no persistence. The posterior puts phi at about three quarters, and the model passes the check. The slope moves as well as widening, because the likelihood now compares each year with what the year before predicts, so the information comes more from changes from one year to the next than from the level of a year against the decade mean of its country. ::: ## Hands-on 2 – Persistence held fixed {#hands-on-2-persistence-held-fixed .smaller} ::: {.small} **In the workspace**, in the console: 1. Fit the two-way regression by generalised least squares, with the persistence held at a value of your choice: ```{.r} euframes <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) fit <- nlme::gls(mcosmo ~ unemp + cntry + factor(year), data = euframes, correlation = nlme::corAR1(0.5, form = ~ year | cntry, fixed = TRUE)) summary(fit)$tTable["unemp", ] ``` 2. Run it with 0, 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95 in place of 0.5, and note the slope and its standard error each time. At 0 the fit is the least-squares slope of the reproduced specification 3. **Which of these comparisons is the claim about, and what does the posterior of φ say about the choice between them?** Two sentences for your notes ::: ::: notes The frequentist twin of the model with persistent errors runs in a second, so you can do by hand what the posterior does by averaging. Fit the two-way regression by generalised least squares, with the persistence held at a value of your choice, and note the slope and its standard error. At nought you get the least-squares slope of the reproduced specification. As you raise the value towards one, the comparison shifts from the level of each year against the decade mean of its country towards the change from one year to the next, and the slope moves towards zero while its standard error grows. Then write two sentences: which of these comparisons is the claim, as the paper states it, about, and what does the posterior of phi, about three quarters, say about the choice between them? [state the time] ::: # PART 3 – Partial pooling {#part-3-partial-pooling .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 3 ::: ::: notes Part three returns to the failed check. Persistent errors are one reading of it, and slopes that differ between countries are another, since a country whose own slope is steeper than the average leaves residuals that follow its unemployment from year to year. So the part gives every country a slope of its own. A separate slope for each country, estimated from its ten years alone, learns nothing from the other countries, and one slope for all ignores how the countries differ. Partial pooling lies between the two. Each country slope is a compromise between its own years and the average of all the countries, and the data decide how far each country leans towards the average. ::: ## A slope for each country {#a-slope-for-each-country .smaller} $$ \beta_c = \beta + u_c, \qquad u_c \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2) $$ ::: {.small} - The slope of each country departs from the average by an amount drawn from a distribution, whose spread $\sigma_b$ the model estimates under the prior normal(0, 0.01) - A model without pooling has 'amnesia': "nothing learned about any one category informs estimates for the other categories", whereas multilevel models "remember features of each cluster in the data as they learn about all of the clusters. Depending upon the variation among clusters, which is learned from the data as well, the model pools information across clusters" [@McElreath2020StatisticalRethinkingBayesian, pp. 399–400] - "small ponds are prone to overfitting, and so they receive a bigger dose of the underfit grand mean", while "the larger ponds shrink much less, because they contain more information" (p. 414) ::: ```{.r} # the formula of the model with a slope for each country, in brms mcosmo ~ 0 + cntry + year_f + unemp_within + (0 + unemp_within | cntry) ``` ::: notes A model with a slope for each country lets the slopes depart from the average by amounts drawn from a distribution, whose spread the model estimates along with everything else. McElreath calls the alternative, a separate slope for each country estimated from its own data alone, a model with amnesia: nothing learnt about one country informs the estimate for another. A multilevel model remembers. Each country slope becomes a compromise between the ten years of that country and the average of all the countries, and the compromise leans towards the average where a country holds little information. In McElreath's example, the small ponds get a bigger dose of the grand mean, and the large ponds shrink much less. In our panel, the information about a slope is the variation in unemployment that remains within a country once the year effects are removed, the unequal weights of the first session. ::: ## The country slopes {#the-country-slopes .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="52%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](eu-frames-bayesian_files/figure-revealjs/d3-country-slopes-1.png){width=537.6} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.small} - The countries with little variation in unemployment are drawn most of the way to the average; Greece and Spain keep slopes steeper than the average, and Poland a slope near zero - The spread of the slopes has a posterior median of 0.0057 (95% credible interval 0.0034 to 0.0091), larger than the size of the average slope, −0.0028 - The same model fitted by REML returns a point estimate of the spread, with none of its uncertainty - This model fails the check of persistence too, with a replicated median of 0.02 - With persistent errors added, φ stays at 0.76, and the spread of the slopes shrinks to 0.0014 (95% credible interval 0.00007 to 0.0046), so that the countries are pooled almost completely ::: ::: :::: ::: {.src} companion/bayesian.qmd, section 5. The vertical line marks the posterior median of the average slope. ::: ::: notes Here are the country slopes. The open grey circles are what each country gives on its own ten years, with the year effects shared, and the filled blue circles are the partially pooled slopes, with the countries ordered from the top by how much of the variation in unemployment each holds. Towards the bottom, the small countries scatter widely on their own, and the model draws them most of the way to the average. At the top, Greece and Spain hold most of the information, so they keep slopes steeper than the average, and Poland keeps a slope near zero. The spread of the slopes is larger than the average slope itself, so on this model the countries do not share one slope. A frequentist fit by REML returns a single number for that spread, where the posterior gives its whole distribution. Slopes that differ do not reproduce the persistence of the residuals, though, and this model fails the check of the second part as well. When persistent errors enter the model too, the spread of the slopes nearly vanishes: with ten years for each country, the data distinguish only poorly between slopes that differ and departures that persist. ::: # PART 4 – The result {#part-4-the-result .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 4 ::: ::: notes The last part runs the final check of the workflow and then reads the result. That check, the sensitivity to the priors, asks whether the result rests on a prior that nobody would defend. Its answer holds the one finding of the module that a report would have to state. Then comes the slope under every model of the session, set beside least squares, and the difference between stating the evidence as a probability and classing it by a threshold. The part closes with the workflow as a whole, in the order in which the session ran it. ::: ## Prior sensitivity {#prior-sensitivity .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Model Parameter Prior Likelihood Diagnosis
One slope Slope 0.003 0.094 –
Persistent errors Slope 0.015 0.131 –
Persistent errors Persistence 0.070 0.121 potential prior-data conflict
A slope for each country Slope 0.008 0.037 –
Country slopes and persistence Slope 0.006 0.107 –
Country slopes and persistence Persistence 0.063 0.120 potential prior-data conflict
``` ::: ::: ::: {.small} - priorsense reweights the draws as if the prior, or the likelihood, were raised to a power slightly above or below 1, "a way to check how sensitive the posterior is to perturbations of the prior and likelihood and diagnose the cause of sensitivity" [@KallioinenEtAl2026PriorsenseEfficientPrior, p. 1] - The slope is insensitive to its prior in every model, between 0.003 and 0.015. The persistence is sensitive, at 0.070 and 0.063: its prior is centred on no persistence, and the data hold a good deal of it ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The prior stays as it was set before the data, and the conflict is reported. It leaves the slope, the quantity of the claim, untouched, and a report of the persistence for its own sake would have to defend its prior as well as its data. ::: ::: notes Comparing fits under different priors answers the question of sensitivity for the priors that you compare. The priorsense package asks it for every prior near the one that was chosen, without fitting the model again: it reweights the draws as if the prior, or the likelihood, had been raised to a power a little above or below one, and measures how far the posterior moves. The slope barely moves with its prior in any model, well under the threshold of point nought five, so its posterior is driven by the data. The persistence is another matter. Its prior is centred on no persistence, the data hold a good deal of it, and priorsense reports a potential conflict between the two. [advance] I keep the prior as it was set before the data and report the conflict. The conflict leaves the slope untouched, and it tells us that the persistence, reported for its own sake, would need its prior defended as well as its data. ::: ## The slope across the models {#the-slope-across-the-models .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](eu-frames-bayesian_files/figure-revealjs/d3-slope-intervals-1.png){width=912} ::: ::: ::: {.small} - The model that passes the posterior predictive check, with persistent errors and a slope for each country, puts the average slope at **−0.00275**, with a 95% credible interval from −0.00550 to +0.00002 - Its probability that the slope is negative is 0.975, and that the slope is steeper than −0.001, a fall of at least one point of share for a rise of ten points of unemployment, 0.896 ::: ::: notes Here is the slope under every model of the session, in points of share for each point of unemployment. The two squares at the top are least squares: the conventional interval, clearly below zero, and the CR2 interval, which ends at zero. The circles are the four posteriors. The model with one slope sits with the conventional interval, because it shares its assumption. The three models that allow for the dependence all centre a little nearer zero, and their intervals end near zero. The model with both terms, persistent errors and a slope for each country, puts the probability that the slope is negative at ninety-seven and a half per cent, and the probability of a fall of at least one point of share for ten points of unemployment at about ninety per cent. The two approaches agree on the main point: once the dependence of the years enters the analysis, the evidence for a negative slope is much weaker than the conventional fit suggests. ::: ## A probability and a threshold {#a-probability-and-a-threshold .smaller} ::: {.small} - The CR2 test classes the reproduced specification as not significant at 5%, with p = 0.0504 on 9.77 df, a margin of 0.04 of a percentage point - "only a small change is required to move an estimate from a 5.1% significance level to 4.9%, thus moving it into statistical significance" [@GelmanStern2006DifferenceSignificantNot, p. 328] - The posterior states the same evidence as a probability that the slope is negative, 0.975, around a central value smaller than the least-squares slope, and it leaves to the reader the judgement of whether a probability of that size is enough for the claim ::: ::: notes The two approaches differ in what each makes of that evidence. The test draws a line, and the reproduced specification falls on the side of not significant at five per cent, by four hundredths of a percentage point. Gelman and Stern pointed out how little separates the two sides of such a line: a small change moves an estimate from a significance level of five point one per cent to four point nine. The posterior draws no line. It states the evidence as a probability that the slope is negative, about ninety-seven and a half per cent here, around a central value smaller than the least-squares slope, and it leaves you to judge whether a probability of that size is enough for the claim. In your report this afternoon you state your own result under the errors that you declared, and this is the language for saying what it means. ::: ## The workflow {#the-workflow .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. **Before the data**: priors on scales that can be read, and the prior predictive check 2. **The computation**: R-hat, the effective sample sizes and the divergent transitions of every model 3. **The fit to the data**: posterior predictive checks on a statistic for a grouping that the model leaves out, here the years of a country, and on the bounds of a share. Not one of the replicated cell means of the final model falls outside 0 to 1, and the observed cell means run from 0.30 to 0.66 4. **The priors again**: power-scaling of the prior and of the likelihood, and a report of any conflict ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The most direct checks compare simulations with "a summary statistic computed from the data or subgroups of the data, especially for groupings not included in the model" [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow, p. 142]. ::: ::: notes Here is the order in which the session ran the checks, which is the order of the workflow that Gelman and colleagues set out in their book. Before the data, priors that can be read, and a simulation of what they imply. Then the computation, model by model. Then the fit to the data, on a statistic chosen for what the model leaves out, here the grouping of the years by country. The final model also respects the bounds of a share, since not one of its replicated cell means leaves the interval from nought to one. And then the priors again, with power-scaling. [advance] The failed posterior predictive check did the most work of the four, because both of the models that followed it, the persistent errors and the slope for each country, were readings of its failure. A posterior is worth reading once all four steps have passed, and a report says what each of them found. ::: ## The reading and the next session {#the-reading-and-the-next-session .smaller} ::: {.small .nonincremental} - **The reading**: [Bayesian estimation](../companion/bayesian.html), the module of the companion curriculum behind this session, with the brms code of every model, the frequentist twins that run on the page, and the task of persistence held fixed. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
